title: Michigan tells Trev Alberts he will not be its athletic director, his lawyer says
dek: Six days after reports that Alberts would leave Texas A&M for Michigan, his attorney says Michigan's search firm has told him the job is not his. Michigan has not said why.
what: On 24 November 2026, ESPN's Pete Thamel reported that Trev Alberts has been told by the search firm working for the University of Michigan that he will not be its next athletic director. The source for this is Alberts's attorney, Tom Mars. Mars says Alberts got phone calls from the firm on Monday night and again on Tuesday morning.

Thamel's post says Alberts signed a "contractually binding MOU" for the job, and that it requires Michigan to pay his full contract buyout. KBTX, the Texas television station, reports that the buyout he owes Texas A&M is $4 million and that, per a post by ESPN's Dan Wetzel, Michigan owes Alberts about $17.3 million under the memorandum. I did not see the memorandum. These figures rest on the lawyer's account as relayed by reporters.
On 18 November, reports said Alberts had agreed to leave Texas A&M, where he has been athletic director since 2024, to lead Michigan. Warde Manuel left the Michigan job earlier this year.

No reason has been given to Alberts, according to his attorney. Reports say his candidacy drew attention after remarks he made in a deposition in a Title IX case in Nebraska, where he used to be athletic director. KBTX says it is not clear whether the lawsuit or the testimony played a part in the decision. Fox 2 Detroit says Alberts's statement to ESPN says Michigan's general counsel spoke with the general counsel of Texas A&M and of the University of Nebraska, and that all three told Michigan he did nothing wrong. I could not open Alberts's statement itself, and I have not seen the deposition.
I found no statement from Michigan in the coverage I read. Texas A&M has named John Thornton interim athletic director from 1 December and has hired a search firm, per KBTX.
why: A hire that looked done has come undone before it began, and a signed agreement means money may change hands. College sports readers also want to know who now runs two big programs' athletic departments.
next: Whether Michigan or the university's governing board comments, whether the memorandum is disputed, and who Michigan names instead. Only Alberts's side has spoken so far.
